## E-commerce Product Photography Checklist: What to Plan Before the Shoot

A reliable e-commerce product photography checklist should cover more than camera equipment: it must include product preparation, shot types, brand consistency, platform requirements, styling, file delivery and usage rights. For Indian businesses, the shoot should also account for marketplaces such as Amazon, Flipkart and Myntra, D2C websites, social media formats, GST-inclusive pricing displays and customer expectations around accurate product representation.

Good product photography helps shoppers understand what they are buying before they contact you or place an order. It cannot compensate for a poor product, unclear pricing or weak fulfilment, but it can reduce confusion and present the product consistently across your website, marketplace listings, catalogues and social channels.

This checklist is designed for D2C brands, small manufacturers, retailers, agencies and businesses planning a product shoot in India.

## 1. Define the Purpose of the Product Shoot

Before booking a photographer, decide where the photographs will be used. A product image made for an Amazon listing may follow different rules from a lifestyle image created for Instagram or a website banner.

A single shoot can support several channels, but only if you plan the required formats in advance. Otherwise, you may receive attractive photographs that do not work for your product page, marketplace gallery or paid advertisements.

### List every intended use

Write down the platforms and placements that matter to your business:

- D2C website product pages
- Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, Meesho or another marketplace
- Instagram posts, Reels covers and Stories
- Facebook and Pinterest
- WhatsApp Business catalogue
- Google Business Profile, where relevant
- Printed brochures, catalogues or retailer sheets
- Paid social media advertisements
- Email campaigns and launch announcements
- Packaging inserts or product education material

For example, a square image may work well for a product grid, while a vertical image may be needed for an Instagram Story. A wide image may be useful for a website banner but unsuitable as the main marketplace image.

### Set the commercial objective

The shoot may be intended to:

- Launch a new product
- Replace inconsistent or outdated images
- Build a complete product catalogue
- Show a new colour or size range
- Explain how the product is used
- Support a festive or seasonal campaign
- Create a bank of social media content
- Improve visual consistency across multiple sales channels

The objective affects the shot list, location, styling and budget. A catalogue shoot requires repeatability. A campaign shoot may need more creative direction, props, models and location planning.

### Prepare a written creative brief

The creative brief does not need to be long. It should answer:

- What is the product?
- Who is the target customer?
- What should the customer notice first?
- What makes the product different?
- What should the images communicate: utility, luxury, simplicity, comfort, freshness or durability?
- Which brands or visual styles are references?
- Where will the images be published?
- What must not appear in the photographs?

Do not copy another brand’s visual identity. References are useful for discussing lighting, composition and mood, but the final work should reflect your own brand.

## 2. Prepare the Products Before Photography

The condition of the products often has more impact on the final images than the camera. Scratches, dust, fingerprints, bent packaging, loose threads and uneven labels become highly visible when a photograph is enlarged on a website.

### Create a product inventory

Make a list of every item that needs to be photographed. Include:

- Product name and internal code
- Variant name
- Colour
- Size
- Pack quantity
- Front and back packaging versions
- New and old versions of the label
- Accessories included in the box
- Products that need model or scale photographs
- Items requiring assembly or demonstration

Use the same names and codes in the inventory, shot list and delivery folders. This reduces the risk of uploading the wrong image to a product page.

### Inspect each product

Check the following before the shoot:

- Surface marks, dents or scratches
- Dust, oil and fingerprints
- Packaging creases and tears
- Correct spelling and placement of labels
- Barcode visibility, if it needs to be shown
- Seals, caps, lids, zips and closures
- Stitching, seams and loose threads
- Colour consistency between product variants
- Correct quantity in each pack
- Included accessories
- Expiry dates or batch information, where relevant

For apparel, steam or iron garments before the shoot. For food, cosmetics and other packaged goods, confirm that the packaging shown is the current version. Do not photograph an old label if the customer will receive a different one.

### Bring duplicate samples where possible

A clean display sample may be needed for hero images, while another unit may be opened, handled or used in a demonstration. Keeping separate samples protects the best product from unnecessary marks.

If the product is fragile, carry extra units. If the product is handmade, identify which variations are intentional and which indicate a defect. The photographer should not have to decide whether an irregularity is part of the product.

### Prepare a styling and prop list

Props should support the product rather than distract from it. A ceramic mug may be shown with a table setting, but the styling should not make the customer think that the plate, spoon or other items are included unless that is clearly explained.

For every prop, ask:

- Is it necessary?
- Does it fit the customer and brand?
- Could it create confusion about what is included?
- Does it make the image easier to understand?
- Will the image still work if the prop is removed for a marketplace listing?

Keep a record of any prop or model used. This helps with reshoots and future campaign content.

## 3. Build a Complete Shot List

A shot list is the central working document for the shoot. It prevents the common problem of receiving one attractive image but missing the practical photographs customers need before purchase.

### Core product photography shots

For most e-commerce products, consider the following:

- Front view
- Back view
- Left side
- Right side
- Top view
- Bottom view, where useful
- Three-quarter angle
- Close-up of texture or finish
- Detail of important features
- Open or unfolded view
- Product with included accessories
- Product shown at a useful scale
- Product in its packaging
- Packaging front, back and side panels
- Product in use
- Group image of a set or bundle
- Comparison of available sizes or variants

Not every product requires every shot. A product photography checklist should be adapted to how customers evaluate that category.

For a skincare product, the back label may matter because it contains ingredients and directions. For a handbag, customers may need to see the inner compartments, strap length and hardware. For furniture, dimensions, underside construction and scale are important.

### Plan the hero image

The hero image is the first photograph a shopper usually sees. It should make the product easy to identify without forcing the viewer to interpret the scene.

For marketplace listings, check the platform’s current image rules before the shoot. Requirements can vary by category and may change. A plain background may be required for the main image, while lifestyle or infographic images may be allowed in later positions.

For a D2C website, a clean hero image may be combined with a branded background, but the product should still be immediately visible. Avoid placing important edges too close to the frame because images may be cropped on mobile devices.

### Add scale and usage images

Customers may not understand size from a product-only photograph. Use a person, hand, household object or familiar setting when it helps communicate scale. The choice should be appropriate to the product and its buyer.

Usage photographs can answer practical questions:

- How is the product worn?
- How does it open?
- How much can it hold?
- How is it installed?
- How does it fit into a room?
- What does the texture look like when used?
- Which parts are removable or adjustable?

Do not use an image to imply performance that the product cannot deliver. Product images and captions should remain consistent with the actual specifications and approved claims.

### Capture social media content during the same session

A planned product shoot can create more than listing images. Capture additional content such as:

- Vertical product images for Stories and Reels covers
- Behind-the-scenes photographs
- Packaging and unboxing frames
- Detail shots for carousel posts
- Founder or maker interactions, if relevant
- Images showing the product in a seasonal setting
- Blank-space compositions for text overlays
- Before-and-after images only where the comparison is genuine and permitted
- Short clips for product demonstrations

Still photographs and video require different planning. If video is important, include it in the brief instead of assuming that a photographer will record usable clips during a still shoot.

## 4. Plan the Brand Photography Direction

Product photography should be accurate first and attractive second. Brand photography adds the visual decisions that make a catalogue feel connected: backgrounds, colours, lighting, framing, props, surfaces and human presence.

### Define the visual system

Decide how the following elements will be used across the shoot:

- Background colour
- Surface material
- Lighting direction
- Shadow strength
- Camera angle
- Distance from the product
- Amount of empty space
- Prop style
- Model styling
- Colour treatment
- Retouching level

A handmade homeware brand may choose natural surfaces and soft daylight. A technology product may require controlled reflections and a cleaner, more precise setup. Neither approach is automatically better; the important point is consistency with the product and audience.

### Balance consistency with variety

A catalogue should look related without making every image identical. Use a consistent baseline for product-only images and introduce variety in lifestyle photographs.

For example:

- Keep camera height and background consistent for catalogue shots.
- Use several useful angles rather than repeating one angle.
- Maintain similar lighting across variants.
- Change props only when they help explain usage or create campaign variety.
- Leave space in selected images for website copy or advertising text.

If each product is photographed with a different background, angle and colour treatment, shoppers may feel that the products come from unrelated businesses. This is especially noticeable when a D2C website has a large product range.

### Use colour references

Colour accuracy matters for apparel, paint, home décor, cosmetics, food packaging and other products where the shade influences the purchase decision.

During the shoot:

- Use a controlled lighting setup where possible.
- Keep white balance consistent.
- Avoid mixing light sources that produce different colour casts.
- Photograph similar variants under the same conditions.
- Review the result on more than one screen.
- Compare the image with the physical product before approval.

Screens vary, and no photograph can guarantee that every customer sees an identical colour. Still, careless lighting or aggressive editing can make the difference much worse.

### Plan human representation carefully

If models are used, decide:

- Age range and appearance relevant to the customer
- Clothing and styling
- Hand and nail presentation for close-ups
- Size and fit requirements
- Poses that demonstrate use
- Whether the model’s face is needed
- Model release and usage duration
- Platforms and territories where the images may appear

For Indian audiences, representation should suit the actual market rather than rely on generic stock imagery. The model should also use the product naturally. An awkward pose can create doubt about comfort, size or usability.

## 5. Get the Technical Requirements Right

The technical setup should support the commercial purpose. A technically sharp image can still fail if the product is cropped, distorted or supplied in the wrong format.

### Confirm aspect ratios and crops

Ask for images that can work across:

- Square product grids
- Vertical social placements
- Website banners
- Marketplace galleries
- Mobile product pages
- WhatsApp catalogues
- Paid advertising formats

It is useful to receive a master image with enough space around the product, along with crops prepared for specific placements. Do not stretch a square image into a wide banner. The product may become too small or appear distorted.

### Decide file formats and background needs

Common delivery requirements may include:

- High-resolution JPEG files for online use
- PNG files where transparent backgrounds are necessary
- Web-optimised copies for faster page loading
- TIFF or another high-quality master format for future editing, if required
- Cropped versions for platform uploads
- Transparent cut-outs for design and advertising work

The exact requirements depend on the website, marketplace and design workflow. Confirm them before the shoot rather than requesting a complete conversion later.

### Photograph reflective and transparent products properly

Glass, glossy packaging, metal and transparent products require careful lighting. Reflections can reveal the studio, camera or unwanted objects. Plan for:

- Clean surfaces
- Controlled light sources
- Diffusion
- Polarising solutions where appropriate
- Multiple test frames
- A separate clean plate, if compositing is planned

Discuss whether the final image will be a single photograph or a composite created from multiple exposures. This affects both the shoot and the post-production process.

### Include reference objects only when they help

A ruler, hand or familiar object may explain size, but it can also make the image look less premium or create an inaccurate comparison. If dimensions are important, show them in a clear graphic or specification section as well as through photography.

Do not rely on the photograph to communicate all factual information. Product pages should also include dimensions, material, weight, care instructions, compatibility and other relevant specifications.

## 6. Plan Compliance, Claims and Product Information

Photography is part of the customer-facing product listing. Images must not create a misleading impression about the product, quantity, size, ingredients, results or certification.

### Review regulated and category-specific details

Depending on the product category, review:

- Manufacturer and packer information
- Country of origin
- MRP and other required declarations
- Net quantity
- Ingredients
- Usage directions
- Warnings and precautions
- Expiry or best-before information
- Customer-care details
- Certification marks
- Warranty terms
- Product dimensions and included items

Indian packaging and consumer information requirements can differ by category. Businesses should confirm current obligations under applicable rules, including Legal Metrology requirements where relevant, and obtain professional advice for regulated products.

The image itself should not hide or alter mandatory information if the packaging is being shown for reference. At the same time, a tiny label photograph should not be the only place where essential information is provided.

### Be careful with performance and health claims

Words and visual comparisons such as “instant,” “clinically proven,” “chemical-free,” “100% safe,” “best,” “guaranteed” or “cures” may require evidence or may be unsuitable for the category.

For cosmetics, food, supplements, healthcare products and children’s products, claims need particular care. An image showing dramatic results, a medical-looking setting or a professional uniform can imply a claim even if the caption does not make one.

Advertising and product communication should be reviewed against applicable Indian rules and industry guidance, including the ASCI Code where relevant. If a claim cannot be supported, remove it from the brief rather than expecting the editor to make it less obvious later.

### Make quantity and inclusions clear

A group photograph may show several products while the customer receives only one. If accessories or props are not included, state this clearly near the image or in the product description.

Use labels such as:

- “Set of three”
- “One unit”
- “Accessories shown for styling only”
- “Colour may vary slightly by screen”
- “Includes charging cable”
- “Batteries not included”

The wording must match the actual offer. This is especially important on marketplaces where customers may make a decision from the image gallery before reading all the text.

## 7. Manage the Shoot Day and Post-Production

A well-organised shoot day saves time and reduces missing assets. Assign one person from the business to make decisions and approve product details.

### Use a shoot-day checklist

Before photography begins, confirm:

- All products have arrived
- Variants are labelled
- Samples are clean and ready
- The shot list is available
- Props and styling materials are packed
- Model agreements are completed, where needed
- Locations and permissions are confirmed
- Power, charging and backup arrangements are ready
- Required backgrounds and surfaces are available
- Platform specifications have been reviewed
- The decision-maker is available for approvals

Photograph a reference frame at the start of each product setup. This can help identify the product, variant and styling used later.

### Review images before the shoot ends

A quick review can catch:

- Missing product variants
- Incorrect labels
- Product dust or fingerprints
- Cropping problems
- Distracting reflections
- Visible pins, stands or supports
- Uneven lighting
- Poorly arranged accessories
- Unnatural model poses
- Unwanted brand names in the background

It is cheaper to correct a missed angle while the product and setup are still available than to arrange a separate reshoot.

### Agree on retouching standards

Retouching may include:

- Dust and minor mark removal
- Background cleaning
- Colour correction
- Straightening
- Exposure adjustment
- Small crease reduction
- Reflection control
- Removal of temporary supports

Retouching should not change the product’s actual colour, texture, size, shape or features. For apparel and beauty products especially, excessive editing can create expectations that the delivered product will not meet.

Agree on whether the deliverables include clipping paths, transparent cut-outs, layered files, image composites, colour variants and source files. These may be separate requirements from the final JPEG images.

### Maintain an asset naming system

A practical naming structure might include:

`brand_product_variant_view_channel_version`

For example, use the product code rather than a casual internal nickname. Keep a separate spreadsheet mapping image names to SKUs, product titles and upload locations.

This becomes valuable when you add new products, change a label, replace a marketplace image or brief a social media agency several months later.

## 8. Choose Deliverables That Support E-commerce and Content Planning

The final delivery should be organised for the people who will actually use the assets. A folder of randomly named photographs creates unnecessary work.

### Suggested delivery structure

You can organise files by:

- Product or SKU
- Product-only images
- Lifestyle images
- Detail images
- Packaging images
- Social media crops
- Video clips
- Edited masters
- Web-optimised files
- Approved final files

Include a simple asset sheet containing:

- File name
- Product code
- Variant
- Image type
- Recommended use
- Orientation
- Notes about props or inclusions
- Approval status

### Compare common deliverable choices

| Deliverable | Useful for | What to confirm |
|---|---|---|
| Product-only images | Marketplace listings and catalogue pages | Background, angles, crop and variant coverage |
| Lifestyle images | D2C websites, social media and advertising | Props, models, location and usage rights |
| Detail images | Features, texture, fit and packaging information | Which customer question each image answers |
| Transparent cut-outs | Website design, ads and banners | File format, edge quality and shadow treatment |
| Vertical social crops | Stories, Reels covers and mobile campaigns | Safe space for text and platform cropping |
| Short product videos | Demonstrations and social content | Duration, orientation, audio and editing |
| Source or layered files | Future resizing and design changes | Whether they are included and in which format |

### Confirm usage rights

If models, locations, props, stylists, music or stock elements are involved, confirm how the assets may be used. Important points include:

- Website and marketplace use
- Organic social media use
- Paid advertising
- Print use
- Duration of usage
- Geographic usage
- Agency or partner access
- Editing and cropping permissions
- Renewal requirements

A photograph may be suitable for Instagram but subject to a different agreement for paid advertising or packaging. Put the arrangement in writing before publishing.

### Connect photography to content planning

Create a content calendar while the images are still fresh. A single shoot might support:

- Product launch announcement
- Feature carousel
- “How to use” post
- Care or maintenance post
- FAQ content
- Customer problem and product solution
- Seasonal promotion
- Gift guide
- Founder or maker story
- Packaging and dispatch content

This does not mean repeating the same product image in every post. Use different crops, details and contexts while keeping the product recognisable.

## 9. Budget and Vendor Selection Considerations

The cost of product photography depends on product count, complexity, location, styling, models, equipment, editing, video requirements and usage rights. Market quotes may be structured per product, per day, per setup or as a larger project package.

Ask for a scope-based quotation rather than comparing only a single day rate.

### Questions to ask a photographer or studio

- Have you photographed similar product categories?
- Will you follow a provided shot list?
- Who handles styling and props?
- Are models, makeup or locations included?
- How many edited images are included?
- Are revisions included?
- Will images be supplied in web-ready and high-resolution formats?
- Can you provide transparent cut-outs?
- Are vertical and square crops included?
- Is video available?
- What is the delivery process?
- Who owns the final images?
- What usage rights are included?
- How are reshoots handled if a product or label is incorrect?
- Will source files be supplied?
- How will GST be shown on the invoice?

GST treatment and invoicing depend on the service provider and transaction details. Ask for a proper invoice and keep it with the project records, particularly if the business is claiming eligible input tax credit.

A lower quote may exclude styling, retouching, image resizing, model usage or commercial rights. A higher quote may include a more complete production service. Compare the deliverables and exclusions, not just the headline amount.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How many photographs should each product have?

There is no universal number. Start with the customer’s questions: what the product looks like from different sides, how large it is, how it is used, what is included and which details affect the purchase. A simple product may need fewer images than apparel, furniture, electronics or cosmetics with multiple important features.

### Should e-commerce product images have a white background?

A clean, neutral background is commonly useful for product listings because it keeps attention on the item and supports catalogue consistency. Marketplace rules can differ, so check the current requirements for your category. Lifestyle images can use branded settings, but they should complement rather than replace the clear product views customers need.

### Can one product shoot be used for Amazon, a website and Instagram?

Yes, if the shoot is planned for all three uses. Tell the photographer the required orientations, crops, background treatments, file sizes and usage rights before production. A shoot planned only for a marketplace may not provide enough vertical content or blank space for social media and website design.

### How can a small business keep product photography affordable?

Begin with the products and channels that generate the most business, then create a focused shot list. Group products with similar backgrounds and lighting setups, prepare all samples in advance and capture a few useful social formats during the same session. Avoid paying for elaborate props or locations that do not help customers understand the product.

### Should the brand edit product photos internally?

Internal teams can manage basic cropping, resizing and file organisation if they have a consistent process. Colour correction, reflections, complex background removal and composites are better handled by someone with the right experience. In either case, keep an approved master file and document the editing standards.

### When should product photography be updated?

Update images when the packaging, formula, colour, design, size, accessories or product contents change. You may also need new photography when the current images no longer explain the product clearly or do not work in the formats used by your current channels. Do not keep showing an older version after the customer has started receiving a different one.

## Where to Start

Begin with a product inventory, the platforms where each image will be used and a written list of customer questions. Next, prepare a shot list covering product-only, detail, usage, packaging and social media content, then confirm technical specifications, compliance information, usage rights and delivery formats with the photographer.

Review a quotation by its scope rather than its day rate, and ask for a clear record of file names, variants, crops and approvals.
